claim: Tactile information conveyed by four classes of low-threshold mechanoreceptor afferent units in fingertips is fundamental for manipulation activities.
source: In particular, tactile information conveyed by the four classes of low-threshold mechanoreceptor afferent units in the fingertips (Johnson et al., 2000; Johnson, 2001; Vallbo and Johansson, 1984a; Abraira and Ginty, 2013) is fundamental for manipulation activities (Edin et al., 1992; Edin and Johansson, 1995).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research establishing this relationship.

claim: Biological sensors innervating glabrous skin can provide information about contact onset, grasping force level, and discrimination of textural features.
source: In addition, the biological sensors innervating the glabrous skin can provide complex types of information such as the onset of the contact with an object, the level of performed grasping force, and discrimination of textural features (Weber et al., 2013; Darian-Smith et al., 1980a).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Providing a sense of touch is the missing milestone in hand prosthesis development.
source: In fact, even though a significant research in biology, medicine and engineering has produced artificial hands that progressively approached the performance of a "natural hand", it is a shared belief that providing a sense of touch is still the missing milestone (Kwok, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation and represents a consensus view in the field.

claim: The MNT process was tested in four intact subjects using percutaneous electrical microstimulation of the median nerve.
source: The MNT approach was initially tested in four intact volunteers using percutaneous electrical microstimulation of the median nerve (Vallbo et al., 1984b; Torebjörk and Ochoa, 1980) (Figure 1a, Figure 2).
evidence: The claim describes the experimental procedure performed in the study, with reference to figures showing the setup.

claim: Intact subjects achieved discrimination ability above 77% (107/138) during the 3AFC psychophysical procedure via percutaneous electrical microstimulation.
source: Microstimulation allowed users to reach discrimination ability above 77% (107/138, Figure 1c, Figure 3a) during a three-alternative forced-choice (3AFC) psychophysical procedure (Perez et al., 2010; Gibson and Craig, 2005) mediated by the artificial touch system, which is based on the use of a MEMS sensor embedded into a human-sized robotic fingertip (Video 1).
evidence: The claim presents experimental results with specific performance metrics and references to figures showing the data.

claim: The capability to discriminate between two sides of surface pairs was correlated with the difference between their spatial periods.
source: The capability to discriminate between the two sides of the surface pairs was correlated with the difference between their spatial periods (Figure 3c).
evidence: The claim describes a correlation found in the experimental data, with reference to a figure showing this relationship.

claim: Event-related potentials after substitutive electrical and natural mechanical stimulation conditions did not reveal any statistical difference.
source: Event-related potentials (Figure 4a) after substitutive electrical (n = 4, estimated power 0.75, Figure 4—figure supplement 2) and natural mechanical stimulation (n = 4, estimated power 0.79, Figure 4—figure supplement 3) conditions did not reveal any statistical difference (Montecarlo statistics with cluster correction for multiple comparisons).
evidence: The claim presents statistical analysis results comparing two stimulation conditions, with reference to figures showing the data.

claim: Primary sensorimotor areas in the hemisphere contralateral to the stimulus presented a significant reduction in clustering coefficient following the incoming sensory stimulus, regardless of its tactile or substitutive nature.
source: Indeed, the primary sensorimotor areas in the hemisphere contralateral to the stimulus presented a significant reduction (3-way ANOVA followed by Duncan's multiple range test, F(1,6) = 6.48, p<0.05, comparison to the ipsilateral hemisphere) in the clustering coefficient following the incoming sensory stimulus, regardless of its tactile or substitutive nature (Figure 4c).
evidence: The claim presents statistical analysis results with specific test statistics and p-values, with reference to a figure.

claim: Generator sources of short-latency components of SEPs elicited by substitutive electrical stimulation were localized at the Postcentral Gyrus (Brodmann Areas 2 and 3).
source: Moreover, the generator sources of short-latency components of Somatosensory Evoked Potentials (SEPs) that were elicited by the substitutive electrical stimulation were localized at the Postcentral Gyrus (Brodmann Areas 2 and 3), which was consistent with a physiological tactile activation of the primary somatosensory cortex (Figure 5), as previously described using a hand area functional source separation method (Di Pino et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim presents localization results from SEP analysis, with reference to a figure and citation to methodology.

claim: The stimulation threshold was similar for microneedle and TIME interfaces (statistically non-different: p>0.05, Kruskal-Wallis test).
source: The model, which takes into account realistic anatomical (Jabaley et al., 1980) and neurophysiological (Vallbo et al., 1984) data, indicated that the stimulated portion of axonal population (Figure 7), and, therefore, the type of sensation, together with the stimulation threshold (statistically non-different: p>0.05, Kruskal-Wallis test) were similar for the two interfaces.
evidence: The claim presents statistical comparison results from computational modeling, with reference to a figure.

claim: The range of electric charge necessary for recruitment was comparable for both microneedle and TIME interfaces.
source: The range of electric charge necessary for recruitment in both cases was comparable (Figure 7, Figure 8).
evidence: The claim presents modeling results comparing the two interfaces, with reference to figures showing the data.

claim: Subject DAS achieved 77/80 correct trials (96%) in the 3AFC psychophysical protocol using TIME stimulation.
source: DAS showed to be able to comply with the entire 3AFC psychophysical protocol via neural stimulation, without any visual input or guidance by the experimenter, and without interruption in each session, and in 77/80 trials (Figure 1c, Figure 9a) of trials he was able to correctly identify whether the two sides of the surface had the same SP or which one had a larger SP (Figure 10).
evidence: The claim presents experimental results with specific performance metrics for the amputee subject, with reference to figures.

claim: DAS reported sensations elicited by temporal modulation of spiking electrical stimulation as pertaining to the palmar side of the index finger of the missing hand.
source: The sensations elicited by temporal modulation of spiking electrical stimulation of the median nerve through a single implanted electrode were reported by DAS as pertaining to the palmar side of the index finger of the missing hand and as providing a realistic representation of the mechanical alternation between ridges and gaps of the experimented gratings (Video 1).
evidence: The claim reports subjective perceptual experience of the amputee subject, with reference to a video.

claim: The discrimination ability obtained using TIME stimulation was higher than the one with microstimulation.
source: These results indicate that the discrimination ability obtained using TIME stimulation was higher than the one with microstimulation (Figure 1c, Figure 3).
evidence: The claim compares performance between two experimental conditions, with reference to figures showing the data.

claim: The higher discrimination performance with TIME stimulation was attributed to prolonged use/training of the implanted neural interface before the present study.
source: This was attributed to the prolonged use/training of the implanted neural interface before the present study (Raspopovic, 2014).
evidence: The claim provides an interpretation of the observed performance difference, with citation to prior work.

claim: The behavioral performance as a function of stimulus in subject DAS can be fit exactly (R = 1) using a logistic function of the difference of SPs between the two halves of each surface.
source: The behavioral performance as a function of stimulus in subject DAS can be fit exactly (R = 1) using a logistic function of the difference of SPs between the two halves of each surface (Figure 9c).
evidence: The claim presents a statistical modeling result with a perfect fit, with reference to a figure.

claim: The MNT process led to linear correlation between the stimulus SP of each texture and a highly specific IBI (ANOVA test, Tukey Kramer correction for multiple comparisons, p<0.00001).
source: Indeed, the MNT process led to linear correlation between the stimulus SP of each texture and a highly specific IBI (ANOVA test, Tukey Kramer correction for multiple comparisons, p<0.00001) reproducing neurophysiological findings in non-human (Darian-Smith et al., 1980a; Phillips and Johnson, 1981) and human (Oddo et al., 2011b) primate studies with similar gratings.
evidence: The claim presents statistical analysis results with specific test statistics and p-values, and cites prior neurophysiological studies.

claim: The difference in IBI between the MNT output elicited by the two sides of each stimulus correlated almost perfectly (R² = 0.997) with the difference in SP.
source: Consequently, the difference in IBI between the MNT output that was elicited by the two sides of each stimulus correlated almost perfectly (R2 = 0.997) with the difference in SP (Figure 9d).
evidence: The claim presents a correlation analysis result with a very high R² value, with reference to a figure.

claim: DAS behavioral responses were perfectly (R = 1) fit by a logistic function of the difference in IBI.
source: Additionally, the behavioral responses of DAS were perfectly (R = 1) fit by a logistic function of the difference in IBI.
evidence: The claim presents a statistical modeling result with a perfect fit.

claim: The AFRs of responses to 0.5, 1.0 and 1.5 mm were not significantly different.
source: In particular, the AFRs of responses to 0.5, 1.0 and 1.5 mm were not significantly different, and the AFRs of responses to 2.0 mm and 3.0 mm were not significantly different (p<0.05 ANOVA test with multiple comparisons).
evidence: The claim presents statistical analysis results comparing average firing rates across different stimuli.

claim: The difference ΔAFR in AFR between the two sides of a stimulus correlated very weakly with the difference between their SP (R² = 0.066 for ΔAFR vs R² = 0.997 for ΔIBI).
source: Consequently, the difference ΔAFR in AFR between the two sides of a stimulus correlated very weakly with the difference between their SP (R2 = 0.066 for ΔAFR vs R2 = 0.997 for ΔIBI, compare Figure 9e and Figure 9d).
evidence: The claim presents a comparison of correlation strengths between two different neural coding schemes, with reference to figures.

claim: No logistic function of the difference in AFR was able to fit DAS behavioral responses (R² = 0.04, p = 0.8).
source: Note that no logistic function of the difference in AFR was able to fit DAS behavioral responses (R2 = 0.04, p = 0.8), which was a significant contrast with the perfect fit achieved with ΔIBI.
evidence: The claim presents statistical modeling results showing poor fit for rate-based coding.

claim: The rate code was not responsible for the subject perception of the presented textures.
source: Therefore, because the total spike count was not able to encode differences between stimuli to a degree compatible with behavioral responses, we concluded that the rate code was not responsible for the subject perception of the presented textures.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the analysis of behavioral and neural data.

claim: The subject exploited the temporal structure of the response to discriminate the stimuli.
source: This further strengthens the hypothesis that the subject exploited the temporal structure of the response to discriminate the stimuli.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation based on the analysis showing poor fit for rate coding and good fit for temporal coding.

claim: When sliding occurs at fixed velocity, the temporal structure of the sensor output is a linear transformation of the spatial structure of the texture.
source: Indeed, it is already known that, when sliding occurs at fixed velocity, the temporal structure of the sensor output is a linear transformation of the spatial structure of the texture (Oddo et al., 2011b; 2011c) , at least for regular textures such as those considered here.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work establishing this relationship.

claim: Recent neuroprosthetic studies showed that pressure sensation can be elicited by injecting a train of pulses with a fixed shape and different frequencies via intrafascicular or cuff interfaces.
source: Recent neuroprosthetic studies showed that pressure sensation can be elicited by injecting a train of pulses with a fixed shape and different frequencies via intrafascicular (Dhillon and Horch, 2005) or cuff (Tan et al., 2014; Ortiz-Catalan et al., 2014) interfaces.
evidence: The claim summarizes prior research findings with citations.

claim: Reconstruction of tactile sensation of force levels and object shape was shown using multi-electrode stimulation via pulses with current amplitude linearly increasing with sensor outputs.
source: Additionally, reconstruction of tactile sensation of force levels and object shape was shown using multi-electrode stimulation via pulses with current amplitude linearly increasing with sensor outputs (Raspopovic, 2014).
evidence: The claim summarizes prior research findings with a citation.

claim: This work focused on eliciting textural features by injecting a biomimetic temporal structure of pulse trains with a fixed current amplitude in each experimental session.
source: In contrast, this work focused on eliciting textural features by injecting a biomimetic (Saal and Bensmaia, 2015) temporal structure of pulse trains with a fixed current amplitude in each experimental session.
evidence: The claim describes the approach taken in the current study, distinguishing it from prior work.

claim: The range of tested tactile stimuli in the current work is on the order of millimeters (0.5–3.0 mm).
source: The range of tested tactile stimuli in the current work is on the order of millimeters (0.5–3.0 mm).
evidence: The claim describes the experimental parameters used in the study.

claim: The tested stimuli pertain to the lower boundary (towards the fine region) of stimuli that are typically classified as coarse.
source: Thus, these stimuli pertain to the lower boundary (towards the fine region) of stimuli that are typically classified as coarse (Weber et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim characterizes the stimuli used in the study with reference to established classification.

claim: Texture discrimination can be artificially provided to users using both needle microstimulation in intact subjects and implantable intraneural interfaces in a transradial amputee.
source: The results of this study show that the texture discrimination skills can be artificially provided to users using both needle microstimulation in intact subjects and implantable intraneural interfaces in a transradial amputee.
evidence: The claim summarizes the main findings of the study.

claim: Both in needle and TIME-based experiments, the subjects were able to use 'artificial' feedback to perform a 3AFC psychophysical test with very good and comparable performance.
source: Both in needle and TIME-based experiments, the subjects were able to use our 'artificial' feedback to perform a 3AFC psychophysical test with very good and comparable performance.
evidence: The claim summarizes the behavioral results across both experimental conditions.

claim: The similarity between the needle and TIME-based stimulations was predicted by the hybrid FEM-biophysical model.
source: The similarity between the needle and TIME-based stimulations was predicted by our hybrid FEM-biophysical model, which supported the transition from acute preparation towards chronically implanted electrodes.
evidence: The claim describes how computational modeling supported the experimental design.

claim: Model predictions were confirmed by the quasi-perfect discrimination (96% overall stimuli) achieved by DAS amputee with TIME stimulation.
source: Furthermore, model predictions were confirmed by the quasi-perfect discrimination (96% overall stimuli, see Figure 1c, and see Figure 9a,b for the analysis on a per-stimulus basis) that was achieved by DAS amputee with TIME stimulation.
evidence: The claim describes how experimental results validated computational model predictions.

claim: A temporal neuronal coding of spatial structure can successfully elicit tactile cues in case of coarse surfaces explored under a passive-dynamic-touch protocol with constant sliding velocity and regulated load force.
source: The results of the present study showed that a temporal neuronal coding of spatial structure (Weber et al., 2013) can successfully elicit tactile cues in case of coarse surfaces that were explored under a passive- dynamic-touch protocol with a constant sliding velocity and a regulated load force, thus, involving controlled motion of the tactile stimulus while the fingertip was not moving (Yoshioka et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim summarizes the main finding regarding neural coding strategy, with citations to relevant literature.

claim: The passive-touch framework allows decoupling of cutaneous information from kinaesthetic afferent sensory feedback and efference copy associated with movement dynamics.
source: In such passive-touch framework there is a lack of voluntary movement. This allows decoupling of cutaneous information (which was our interest in this study) from the kinaesthetic afferent sensory feedback and efference copy associated with movement dynamics.
evidence: The claim explains the rationale for the experimental design choice.

claim: No significant differences in topography or frequency modulation clustering were shown by the EEG signals between substitutive neuromorphic electrical stimulation and natural mechanical tactile stimulation.
source: Thus, it was possible to compare the EEG activities evoked by the substitutive neuromorphic electrical stimulation versus the natural mechanical tactile stimulation. No significant differences in topography or frequency modulation clustering were shown by the EEG signals in the two cases.
evidence: The claim summarizes the EEG analysis results comparing the two stimulation modalities.

claim: Injecting the sensor output via a single stimulation channel was sufficient to induce accurate responses in the designed experimental protocol with locked indentation force and tangential velocity of stimulus pairs.
source: The behavioral results showed that injecting the sensor output via a single stimulation channel was sufficient to induce accurate responses (particularly from DAS) in the designed experimental protocol with locked indentation force and tangential velocity of stimulus pairs.
evidence: The claim summarizes a key finding about the sufficiency of single-channel stimulation under controlled conditions.

claim: For more complex texture discriminating tasks, integration of spatiotemporal information from neighboring receptors distributed along the fingertip and multi-channel stimulation combined with amplitude modulation would be needed in less restrictive conditions.
source: However, for more complex texture discriminating tasks it is plausible that integration of spatiotemporal information from neighboring receptors distributed along the fingertip (Johansson and Flanagan, 2009; Jörntell et al., 2014) and, thus, multi-channel stimulation, combined with amplitude modulation (Raspopovic, 2014), would be needed in less restrictive conditions that involve velocity or force variations and everyday life stimuli (Weber et al., 2013; Dépeault et al., 2008; Rongala et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is a speculation about future requirements based on the current findings and cited literature.

claim: Neuromorphic stimulation could be a natural and effective tool for eliciting texture discrimination abilities via hand prostheses.
source: The promising results obtained with microstimulation in four intact subjects, combined with robust translational indications from the hybrid model and an excellent outcome from one amputee, prompt the idea that neuromorphic stimulation could be a natural and effective tool for eliciting texture discrimination abilities via hand prostheses.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the combined results of the study.

claim: Neuroprosthetic research can contribute to the evaluation of open neuroscientific hypotheses about tactile perception for the advancement of understanding of human somatosensory physiology.
source: Neuroprosthetic research (Tan et al., 2014; Raspopovic, 2014; Dhillon and Horch, 2005; Rossini et al., 2010) can in parallel contribute to the evaluation of open neuroscientific hypotheses about tactile perception (Weber et al., 2013; Yoshioka et al., 2001; Johansson and Flanagan, 2009; Hollins and Risner, 2000) for the advancement of understanding of human somatosensory physiology.
evidence: The claim discusses the broader implications of neuroprosthetic research with citations to relevant literature.

claim: The MEMS sensor has 4 transducing piezoresistors implanted at the base of a cross-shaped structure.
source: The core element of the artificial fingertip was a Micro Electro Mechanical System (MEMS) sensor with 4 transducing piezoresistors implanted at the base of a cross-shaped structure (Beccai et al., 2005) (Figure 3).
evidence: The claim describes the technical specifications of the sensor used in the study.

claim: The Izhikevich spiking neuron model was originally conceived to emulate neuron-to-neuron signaling.
source: Such model was originally conceived to emulate neuron-to-neuron signaling, whereas in this modified implementation the input is haptic rather than synaptic.
evidence: The claim describes the original purpose of the model and how it was adapted for this study.

claim: The MNT process emulated to some extent the neural representation of stimulus spatial patterning observed in previous non-human and human primate recordings of SA1 afferents associated to Merkel mechanoreceptors.
source: The MNT process emulated to some extent the neural representation of stimulus spatial patterning observed in previous non-human (Weber et al., 2013; Darian-Smith et al., 1980a) and human (Oddo et al., 2011b) primate recordings of SA1 afferents associated to Merkel mechanoreceptors, a functionally relevant class of tactile units able to encode medium-coarse textures (Weber et al., 2013; Phillips and Johnson, 1981; Yoshioka et al., 2001; Darian-Smith et al., 1980b) such as the surfaces evaluated in the present study.
evidence: The claim describes how the MNT process was designed to mimic biological neural responses, with citations to prior neurophysiological studies.

claim: The resulting firing was characterized by biomimetic bursts of multiple spikes per ridge with coarser surfaces, by triplets or duplets for surfaces with medium coarseness, down to a single spike per ridge with finer surfaces.
source: The resulting firing (Figure 2) was characterized by biomimetic (Sathian et al., 1989) bursts of multiple spikes per ridge with coarser surfaces (see 3.0 mm and 2.0 mm SP in Figure 10), by triplets or duplets for surfaces with medium coarseness (see 1.5 mm and 1.0 mm SP in Figure 10), down to a single spike per ridge with finer surfaces (see 0.5 mm SP in Figure 10), thus implementing a neural code of stimulus geometry based on the modulation of discharge rather than on the mean discharge frequency, resembling SA1 electrophysiological recordings under similar tactile stimulation conditions (Darian-Smith et al., 1980a; Phillips and Johnson, 1981) (Figure 10—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim describes the characteristics of the artificial neural responses with references to figures and citations to biological recordings.

claim: The instantaneous firing rate of the implemented artificial mechanoreceptor model achieves a modulation up to tens of spikes/s, coherently with typical values reported in the literature for SA1 units.
source: Furthermore, the instantaneous firing rate of the implemented artificial mechanoreceptor model achieves a modulation up to tens of spikes/s (see red traces in Figure 10), coherently with typical values reported in the literature for SA1 units (Johnson, 2001; Phillips and Johnson, 1981).
evidence: The claim compares the artificial system's firing rates to biological values from the literature.

claim: Four intact subjects (2 males and 2 females, 25–26 years old) underwent the experiments of texture discrimination with tactile feedback elicited by stimulation injected through two microneurographic electrodes.
source: Four intact subjects (2 males and 2 females, 25–26 years old) underwent the experiments of texture discrimination with tactile feedback elicited by a stimulation injected through two microneurographic electrodes (FHC UNP40GAS, shaped as needles).
evidence: The claim describes the participant demographics and experimental setup.

claim: The enrolment was subjected to signing a written Informed Consent, approved by the Campus Bio-Medico University Ethics Committee.
source: The enrolment was subjected to signing a written Informed Consent, approved by the Campus Bio-Medico University Ethics Committee, where this set of experiments took place.
evidence: The claim describes the ethical approval for the study.

claim: Participant DAS had suffered a traumatic transradial left arm amputation 10 years before the experiments.
source: Participant DAS had suffered a traumatic transradial left arm amputation 10 years before the experiments.
evidence: The claim provides background information about the amputee participant.

claim: DAS was selected from a group of 31 persons with hand amputation because of the stump characteristics and his psychophysical abilities.
source: He was selected from a group of 31 persons with hand amputation because of the stump characteristics and his psychophysical abilities.
evidence: The claim describes the selection criteria for the amputee participant.

claim: All procedures were approved by the Institutional Ethics Committees of Policlinic A. Gemelli at Catholic University, IRCCS S. Raffaele Pisana (Rome), the Ethics Committee of Campus Bio-Medico University and the Italian Ministry of Health.
source: All procedures were approved by the Institutional Ethics Committees of Policlinic A. Gemelli at Catholic University, where the surgery was performed, IRCCS S. Raffaele Pisana (Rome), where the experiments were performed, the Ethics Committee of Campus Bio-Medico University and the Italian Ministry of Health.
evidence: The claim describes the ethical approvals for the amputee experiments.

claim: TIME neural interfaces were implanted under general anaesthesia.
source: TIME neural interfaces were implanted under general anaesthesia.
evidence: The claim describes the surgical procedure.

claim: Two TIME electrodes were inserted into the nerve trunk of each nerve (median and ulnar, only the former of which was used for electrical stimulation in the present work).
source: Following an epineurial microdissection, performed under a surgical microscope (Zeiss, Pentero) to visualize the fascicles, two TIME electrodes were inserted into the nerve trunk of each nerve (median and ulnar, only the former of which was used for electrical stimulation in the present work).
evidence: The claim describes the surgical implantation procedure and which electrodes were used in the study.

claim: The electrodes were removed after 30 days, in accordance with EU guidelines.
source: The electrodes were removed after 30 days, in accordance with EU guidelines.
evidence: The claim describes the duration of the implant and regulatory compliance.

claim: At the time of removal, the TIME electrodes were still performing extremely well, and did not cause any discomfort to the subject.
source: At the time of removal however, the TIME electrodes were still performing extremely well, and did not cause any discomfort to the subject.
evidence: The claim reports the functional status and safety of the implanted electrodes at removal.

claim: The follow-up of the clinical condition of the participant almost 2 years after the end of the protocol did not reveal any subjective or objective side effects.
source: The follow-up of the clinical condition of the participant almost 2 years after the end of the protocol did not reveal any subjective or objective side effects.
evidence: The claim reports long-term safety outcomes for the amputee participant.

claim: The tactile stimuli were gratings fabricated with 3D printing of plastic material consisting of a sequence of alternating ridges and grooves with spatial period (SP) from a minimum of 0.5 mm to a maximum of 3.0 mm.
source: The tactile stimuli were gratings, fabricated with 3D printing of plastic material (Project HD 3000, 3D Systems), consisting of a sequence of alternating ridges and grooves with spatial period (SP) from a minimum of 0.5 mm to a maximum of 3.0 mm depending on the stimulus and on the half portion of the surface under test (Figure 1b, Figure 2, Figure 10).
evidence: The claim describes the fabrication and specifications of the tactile stimuli used in the experiments.

claim: The sequence of presented stimuli was randomized within sessions of 16 trials composed of 4 presentations of the 4 surfaces ∆0.0, ∆1.0, ∆2.0 and ∆2.5.
source: The sequence of presented stimuli was randomized within sessions of 16 trials composed of 4 presentations of the 4 surfaces ∆0.0, ∆1.0, ∆2.0 and ∆2.5.
evidence: The claim describes the experimental protocol design.

claim: The 95% confidence intervals for performance estimate from individual subjects responses were computed with exact Clopper Pearson method.
source: The 95% confidence intervals for performance estimate from individual subjects responses were computed with exact Clopper Pearson method (binofit function in Matlab) and compared against chance level (1/3) to assess performance significance.
evidence: The claim describes the statistical methods used for performance analysis.

claim: EEG signals were recorded in all microstimulation sessions using a 64 channel EEG device with a 2 kHz sampling rate.
source: In order to investigate the neural correlates of natural and substitutive texture discrimination, EEG signals were recorded in all microstimulation sessions using a 64 channel EEG device (SD LTM Express, Micromed S.p.A., Italy) with a 2 kHz sampling rate.
evidence: The claim describes the EEG recording equipment and parameters.

claim: The montage was in accordance with the 5% 10/20 system.
source: The montage was in accordance with the 5% 10/20 system (Oostenveld and Praamstra, 2001).
evidence: The claim describes the EEG electrode placement system used, with citation.

claim: Careful scalp preparation granted electrodes impedance below 5 kΩ in at least 90% of derivations, as measured at the experiment onset.
source: Careful scalp preparation granted electrodes impedance below 5 kΩ in at least 90% of derivations, as measured at the experiment onset.
evidence: The claim describes the quality control measures for EEG recording.

claim: EEG signals were processed via independent component analysis (ICA) filtering to remove non-neural sources and artifacts.
source: Data were analyzed by Matlab scripts based on the EEGLAB toolbox (Delorme and Makeig, 2004). EEG signals were processed via independent component analysis (ICA) filtering to remove non-neural sources and artifacts.
evidence: The claim describes the signal processing methods used for EEG analysis.

claim: For subject M4, a realistic head model was obtained using a T1-weighted magnetic resonance (MR) image of the subject and a 4-layer model accounting for scalp, skull, brain tissue, and cerebrospinal fluid.
source: Regarding source localization, for subject M4 a realistic head model was obtained by means of the NFT toolbox (Acar and Makeig, 2010) using a T1-weighted magnetic resonance (MR) image of the subject and a 4-layer model accounting for scalp (σ = 0.33), skull (σ = 0.0132), brain tissue (σ = 0.33), and cerebrospinal fluid (σ = 1.79) respectively.
evidence: The claim describes the methods used for EEG source localization modeling.

claim: The Finite Element Method (FEM) was used for the numerical solution of the forward problem with Boundary Element Method (BEM) meshes as boundaries.
source: The Finite Element Method (FEM) was used for the numerical solution of the forward problem with Boundary Element Method (BEM) meshes as boundaries.
evidence: The claim describes the computational methods used for EEG source localization.

claim: Source localization was performed on the most reliable short-latency potential of cortical origin, namely the P27 peak.
source: Source localization was then performed on the most reliable short-latency potential of cortical origin, namely the P27 peak (Figure 5).
evidence: The claim describes which EEG component was analyzed for source localization.

claim: EEG functional connectivity analysis was performed using the eLORETA exact low-resolution electromagnetic tomography software.
source: EEG functional connectivity analysis was performed using the eLORETA exact low-resolution electromagnetic tomography (Vecchio et al., 2015; Pascual-Marqui, 2011; Vecchio et al., 2014a; 2014b; 2015b) software.
evidence: The claim describes the software and methods used for connectivity analysis.

claim: Brain connectivity was computed with sLORETA/eLORETA software in 7 regions, positioning the center in Brodmann Areas (BAs: 1–7) separately on the left and right hemispheres.
source: To obtain a topographic view of the sensorimotor network, brain connectivity was computed with sLORETA/eLORETA software in 7 regions, positioning the center in Brodmann Areas (BAs: 1–7) separately on the left and right hemispheres.
evidence: The claim describes the regions of interest used for connectivity analysis.

claim: Intracortical Lagged Linear Coherence was computed between all possible pairs of the ROIs for each of the five independent EEG frequency bands: delta (2–4 Hz), theta (4–8 Hz), alpha (8–13 Hz), low beta (13–20 Hz) and high beta (20–30 Hz).
source: For each subject and for each hemisphere, among the eLORETA current density time series of the 7 Regions of Interest (ROIs), intracortical Lagged Linear Coherence, extracted using a sphere with 19 mm of radius (Pascual-Marqui, 2011; 2007) , was computed between all possible pairs of the ROIs for each of the five independent EEG frequency bands: delta (2–4 Hz), theta (4–8 Hz), alpha (8–13 Hz), low beta (13–20 Hz) and high beta (20–30 Hz).
evidence: The claim describes the connectivity metric and frequency bands used in the analysis.

claim: The clustering coefficient characterizes the tendency of the nearest neighbors of a node to be interconnected.
source: The measure considered here was the clustering (C) that characterizes the tendency of the nearest neighbors of a node to be interconnected.
evidence: The claim defines the graph theory metric used in the analysis.

claim: Hybrid models account for the anisotropy of extracellular conductivity during the calculation of the electrical field induced by the injection of electrical current into the tissue and for the nonlinear response of cells to the extracellular stimulation.
source: Hybrid models (Raspopovic et al., 2011; McIntyre et al., 2002) account for the anisotropy of extracellular conductivity during the calculation of the electrical field induced by the injection of the electrical current into the tissue, present in real nerves, and for the nonlinear response of cells to the extracellular stimulation.
evidence: The claim describes the capabilities of hybrid computational models with citations.

claim: An anatomically shaped geometrical model of the median nerve was generated by image segmentation.
source: To do so, an anatomically shaped geometrical model of the median nerve (Jabaley et al., 1980) was generated by image segmentation (ImageJ, USA).
evidence: The claim describes the method used to create the nerve model geometry.

claim: Perineurium had a thickness of 3% of the diameter of the fascicles.
source: Perineurium had a thickness of 3% of the diameter of the fascicles (Grinberg et al., 2008) , and coordinates were interpolated.
evidence: The claim describes an anatomical parameter used in the model, with citation.

claim: The nerve diameter had a maximum of 4.6 mm and minimum of 2.3 mm, as obtained from unpublished histological data provided by Dr. Xavier Navarro and from post-mortem human cadavers dissections at Universitat Autonoma de Barcelona, Spain.
source: The nerve diameter had a maximum of 4.6 mm and minimum of 2.3 mm, as obtained from unpublished histological data provided by Dr. Xavier Navarro and from post-mortem human cadavers dissections at Universitat Autonoma de Barcelona, Spain.
evidence: The claim describes anatomical parameters used in the model based on unpublished data.

claim: MRG model was used to model the nerve tactile sensory fibers.
source: On the biophysical side, MRG model (McIntyre et al., 2002) was used to model the nerve tactile sensory fibers.
evidence: The claim describes the biophysical model used for nerve fibers, with citation.

claim: The MRG model is capable of reproducing several experimental aspects of cells dynamics.

claim: It was assumed that fibers within one fascicle innervate the same hand area.
source: As the fiber organization within different fascicles in the nerve is unknown, we assumed that fibers within one fascicle innervate the same hand area (Jabaley et al., 1980) (i.e., the fibers in one fascicle are innervating a single finger tip and not many of them).

source: Moreover, since there is an inherent anatomical uncertainty in placement and extension of fibers innervating a specific hand district, for every position of stimulating electrode/needle we implemented 9 populations having different extensions and centroids for the same large fascicle (i.e., spanning from having the whole fascicle uniformly populated, to the case of very concentrated population where the fibers are almost touching each-other, Figure 8 and Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim describes how anatomical uncertainty was addressed in the modeling, with reference to figures.
